name: Vent Values
source: Heuer & Rodriguez, Comprehensive Respiratory Therapy Exam Preparation Guide, 4th ed.

cards.q: What 5 criteria must be met before a ventilated patient gets a weaning assessment?
cards.a:
What 5 criteria must be met before a ventilated patient gets a weaning assessment?
1. Some reversal of the underlying cause of respiratory failure
2. Adequate oxygenation — P/F ≥ 150–200, PEEP ≤ 5–8 cm H₂O, FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5
3. pH ≥ 7.25
4. Hemodynamic stability (no myocardial ischemia or significant hypotension)
5. Able to initiate an inspiratory effort

cards.q: Weaning readiness: what P/F, PEEP and FiO₂ count as "adequate oxygenation"?
cards.a:
Weaning readiness: what P/F, PEEP and FiO₂ count as "adequate oxygenation"?
P/F ≥ 150–200
PEEP ≤ 5–8 cm H₂O
FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5

cards.q: What is the minimum pH before starting a weaning assessment?
cards.a:
What is the minimum pH before starting a weaning assessment?
pH ≥ 7.25

cards.q: ARDSNet: which FiO₂ / PEEP combinations make a patient ready for an SBT?
cards.a:
ARDSNet: which FiO₂ / PEEP combinations make a patient ready for an SBT?
FiO₂ ≤ 0.40 and PEEP ≤ 8 cm H₂O
— or —
FiO₂ ≤ 0.50 and PEEP ≤ 5 cm H₂O
…and both no higher than the previous day's settings.

cards.q: ARDSNet SBT readiness — besides FiO₂/PEEP, what 3 other things must be true?
cards.a:
ARDSNet SBT readiness — besides FiO₂/PEEP, what 3 other things must be true?
1. Acceptable spontaneous breathing efforts
2. Systolic BP ≥ 90 mm Hg without vasopressors
3. No neuromuscular blocking agents or blockade

cards.q: ARDSNet: how do you check for acceptable spontaneous breathing effort?
cards.a:
ARDSNet: how do you check for acceptable spontaneous breathing effort?
Decrease the ventilator rate by 50% for 5 minutes and watch for effort.

cards.q: What is the quickest route to getting a patient off the ventilator?
cards.a:
What is the quickest route to getting a patient off the ventilator?
Daily spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs) in patients who meet readiness criteria.

cards.q: VC and MIP/NIF trends, or a monitored SBT — which is the most valid predictor that a patient can stay off the ventilator?
cards.a:
VC and MIP/NIF trends, or a monitored SBT — which is the most valid predictor that a patient can stay off the ventilator?
A carefully monitored SBT. VC and MIP/NIF trends give useful insight, but the SBT is the most valid information.

cards.q: Which 4 spontaneous breathing modes are used for SBTs, and which is best?
cards.a:
Which 4 spontaneous breathing modes are used for SBTs, and which is best?
T-tube · CPAP · pressure support · CPAP + pressure support
No one approach is better than the others. CPAP helps triggering when there is auto-PEEP; PS helps overcome the work of breathing added by the artificial airway.

cards.q: Spontaneous tidal volume: normal adult range, and the critical value?
cards.a:
Spontaneous tidal volume: normal adult range, and the critical value?
Normal 5–7 mL/kg PBW
Critical: < 4–5 mL/kg PBW or < 300 mL

cards.q: Spontaneous respiratory rate: normal adult range, and the critical values?
cards.a:
Spontaneous respiratory rate: normal adult range, and the critical values?
Normal 12–20/min
Critical: < 6/min or > 30–35/min (a second table in the same book lists < 5/min as the low cutoff)

cards.q: Minute ventilation: normal adult range, and the critical values?
cards.a:
Minute ventilation: normal adult range, and the critical values?
Normal 5–10 L/min
Critical: < 4 L/min or > 10 L/min

cards.q: Rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI): formula, normal value, and the value that predicts weaning failure?
cards.a:
Rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI): formula, normal value, and the value that predicts weaning failure?
RSBI = f ÷ VT (in liters)
Normal < 50
> 105 predicts weaning failure
Your course: Chang's slide prints < 100; NBRC exams use 105.

cards.q: Rate 40/min, tidal volume 250 mL. What is the RSBI — and will this patient likely wean?
cards.a:
Rate 40/min, tidal volume 250 mL. What is the RSBI — and will this patient likely wean?
40 ÷ 0.25 L = 160
> 105 → predicts weaning failure (rapid, shallow breathing).

cards.q: Of the bedside weaning measures, which 2 are the BEST indicators that a patient can tolerate spontaneous breathing?
cards.a:
Of the bedside weaning measures, which 2 are the BEST indicators that a patient can tolerate spontaneous breathing?
Respiratory rate and RSBI.
MIP/NIF and VC are used mainly to follow patients with neuromuscular disorders.

cards.q: Deadspace fraction (VD/VT): normal range, and the critical value?
cards.a:
Deadspace fraction (VD/VT): normal range, and the critical value?
Normal 0.25–0.35
Critical: > 0.6–0.7

cards.q: Vital capacity: normal value, and the critical value for weaning?
cards.a:
Vital capacity: normal value, and the critical value for weaning?
Normal 70 mL/kg PBW
Critical: < 10–15 mL/kg PBW

cards.q: MIP / NIF: normal adult value, and the critical value?
cards.a:
MIP / NIF: normal adult value, and the critical value?
Normal −80 to −100 cm H₂O (a second table in the same book lists −80 to −120)
Critical: less negative than −20 to −25 cm H₂O → muscle strength likely too weak to support spontaneous breathing.
Your course: Your weaning deck prints normal −80 to −100; the weaning threshold appears as −20, −20 to −30 and −30 across your decks.

cards.q: How is MIP/NIF measured?
cards.a:
How is MIP/NIF measured?
Maximum pressure generated against an occluded airway at or near RV, during successive inspiratory efforts for 15–25 seconds.

cards.q: Predicted body weight (PBW) formulas for men and women?
cards.a:
Predicted body weight (PBW) formulas for men and women?
Male: PBW (kg) = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60)
Female: PBW (kg) = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60)

cards.q: A 6-foot (72 in) man weighs 120 kg. What is his PBW, and what initial VT range applies?
cards.a:
A 6-foot (72 in) man weighs 120 kg. What is his PBW, and what initial VT range applies?
PBW = 50 + 2.3 × (72 − 60) = 77.6 kg
At 8 mL/kg ≈ 625 mL; the range is 600–800 mL — never 1200 mL. Always use PBW, not actual weight.

cards.q: Unless told otherwise, how much deadspace do you assume per breath?
cards.a:
Unless told otherwise, how much deadspace do you assume per breath?
About 1 mL per pound of predicted body weight.

cards.q: 125-lb patient, rate 15/min, VT 400 mL. What is the alveolar minute ventilation?
cards.a:
125-lb patient, rate 15/min, VT 400 mL. What is the alveolar minute ventilation?
V̇A = f × (VT − VD) = 15 × (400 − 125) = 4125 mL/min (≈ 4.1 L/min)
(deadspace ≈ 1 mL/lb → 125 mL)

cards.q: SBT protocol: how long is the screening phase, and how long is the full trial?
cards.a:
SBT protocol: how long is the screening phase, and how long is the full trial?
Screening: 2–5 minutes of closely monitored spontaneous breathing
Full SBT: at least 30 minutes, no more than 120 minutes

cards.q: SBT success — what gas-exchange values must the patient keep?
cards.a:
SBT success — what gas-exchange values must the patient keep?
SpO₂ ≥ 85–90% or PaO₂ ≥ 50–60 torr
pH ≥ 7.30
PaCO₂ rise ≤ 10 torr

cards.q: SBT success — what heart rate and blood pressure limits apply?
cards.a:
SBT success — what heart rate and blood pressure limits apply?
HR < 120–140/min, change < 20% from baseline
Systolic BP < 180–200 and > 90 mm Hg, change < 20%
No vasopressors

cards.q: SBT success — what breathing-pattern limits apply?
cards.a:
SBT success — what breathing-pattern limits apply?
Respiratory rate ≤ 30–35/min
Change in rate < 50% from baseline

cards.q: Even with good numbers, which subjective signs should make you stop an SBT?
cards.a:
Even with good numbers, which subjective signs should make you stop an SBT?
• Change in mental status (somnolence, coma, agitation, anxiety)
• Onset or worsening discomfort
• Diaphoresis
• ↑ Work of breathing: accessory muscle use, thoracoabdominal paradox

cards.q: A patient fails the SBT. What do you do, and when do you try again?
cards.a:
A patient fails the SBT. What do you do, and when do you try again?
Return the patient to enough support to rest the muscles and maintain oxygenation/ventilation, work with the physician to find the cause, then repeat the SBT every 24 hours.

cards.q: The patient passes the SBT. Does that automatically mean extubate?
cards.a:
The patient passes the SBT. Does that automatically mean extubate?
No. Extubation is a separate decision based on airway patency and protective reflexes.

cards.q: ARDSNet SBT: what settings and how long?
cards.a:
ARDSNet SBT: what settings and how long?
Up to 120 minutes with FiO₂ < 0.5 and PEEP < 5, on a T-piece, trach collar, or CPAP ≤ 5 cm H₂O with PS < 5 cm H₂O. Tolerated ≥ 30 minutes → consider extubation.

cards.q: ARDSNet SBT: which 5 criteria show the patient is tolerating it?
cards.a:
ARDSNet SBT: which 5 criteria show the patient is tolerating it?
1. SpO₂ ≥ 90% and PaO₂ ≥ 60 torr
2. Spontaneous VT ≥ 4 mL/kg PBW
3. RR ≤ 35/min
4. pH ≥ 7.3
5. No respiratory distress

cards.q: ARDSNet SBT: what counts as "respiratory distress"?
cards.a:
ARDSNet SBT: what counts as "respiratory distress"?
2 or more of: HR > 120% of baseline · marked accessory muscle use · abdominal paradox · diaphoresis · marked dyspnea

cards.q: Which 4 conditions must be met before removing a tracheal tube?
cards.a:
Which 4 conditions must be met before removing a tracheal tube?
1. Maintains oxygenation and ventilation without support
2. Minimal risk of upper airway obstruction
3. Adequate airway protection, minimal aspiration risk
4. Can clear secretions on their own

cards.q: How do you do a cuff-leak test, and what does a "positive" test mean?
cards.a:
How do you do a cuff-leak test, and what does a "positive" test mean?
Suction above the cuff, fully deflate the cuff, and occlude the tube outlet. Air leaking around the tube during spontaneous breathing = positive → upper airway likely patent.

cards.q: Which 2 bedside signs show adequate airway protection before extubation?
cards.a:
Which 2 bedside signs show adequate airway protection before extubation?
A positive gag reflex and the ability to lift the head off the bed.

cards.q: What maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) shows the patient can clear secretions?
cards.a:
What maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) shows the patient can clear secretions?
MEP > 60 cm H₂O — plus alert and coughing deeply on suctioning.

cards.q: Stridor develops after extubation. What do you give?
cards.a:
Stridor develops after extubation. What do you give?
Cool, humidified O₂ by aerosol mask and recommend aerosolized racemic epinephrine.

cards.q: What is the most serious complication of extubation, and how do you treat it?
cards.a:
What is the most serious complication of extubation, and how do you treat it?
Laryngospasm. First give positive-pressure ventilation by BVM with 100% O₂. If it persists, the physician may paralyze and reintubate.

cards.q: How long should a patient stay NPO after extubation?
cards.a:
How long should a patient stay NPO after extubation?
24 hours (except sips of water).

cards.q: What cuff pressure range do you keep on a ventilated patient's tube?
cards.a:
What cuff pressure range do you keep on a ventilated patient's tube?
20–30 cm H₂O with no gurgling at peak inspiration. The minimal leak technique is no longer recommended.
Your course: Your deck teaches the minimal leak technique — Heuer says avoid it. Answer to your instructor on the course exam.

cards.q: What happens if cuff pressure is too high? Too low?
cards.a:
What happens if cuff pressure is too high? Too low?
Over 25–30 cm H₂O → blocks tracheal blood flow → ischemia, ulceration, necrosis.
Too low → leakage-type aspiration → VAP.

cards.q: You need > 30 cm H₂O cuff pressure to seal right after intubation — vs needing higher and higher pressure over days. What does each suggest?
cards.a:
You need > 30 cm H₂O cuff pressure to seal right after intubation — vs needing higher and higher pressure over days. What does each suggest?
Right after intubation → tube too small; recommend a proper-size tube.
Rising over time → tracheal dilation/tracheomalacia or a cuff/pilot balloon malfunction.

cards.q: Leakage-type aspiration can't be stopped at a cuff pressure of 30 cm H₂O. What do you recommend?
cards.a:
Leakage-type aspiration can't be stopped at a cuff pressure of 30 cm H₂O. What do you recommend?
Exchange the airway for one with continuous aspiration of subglottic secretions.

cards.q: How often should cuff pressure be checked?
cards.a:
How often should cuff pressure be checked?
Regularly — once per shift — and whenever the tube is changed or moves, air is added/removed, or a leak occurs.

cards.q: Initial tidal volume for full ventilatory support of an adult? And in ARDS?
cards.a:
Initial tidal volume for full ventilatory support of an adult? And in ARDS?
6–8 mL/kg PBW, keeping Pplat ≤ 30–35 cm H₂O
ARDS: 4–6 mL/kg (ARDS protocol)
Your course: Your decks print several VT ranges — older 8–10, 5–10 and < 10 mL/kg; newer 6–8 and 4–6 mL/kg. For ARDS remember ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW.

cards.q: Initial set rate for adult full ventilatory support?
cards.a:
Initial set rate for adult full ventilatory support?
8–24/min (up to 35/min with a low-VT strategy)

cards.q: Initial trigger sensitivity — pressure and flow triggering?
cards.a:
Initial trigger sensitivity — pressure and flow triggering?
Pressure trigger: 1–2 cm H₂O below baseline
Flow trigger: 1–3 L/min below baseline

cards.q: What I:E ratio do you aim for, and why?
cards.a:
What I:E ratio do you aim for, and why?
I:E ≤ 1:1 (e.g., 1:2, 1:3) — enough expiratory time to prevent auto-PEEP. Only inverse-ratio ventilation has TI > TE.

cards.q: Flow waveform setup — volume control vs pressure control?
cards.a:
Flow waveform setup — volume control vs pressure control?
VC: square or decelerating, with enough flow to prevent scalloping (flow starvation) of the pressure curve
PC: adjust rise time to reach a plateau without spiking

cards.q: How much pressure support do you add in SIMV, and why?
cards.a:
How much pressure support do you add in SIMV, and why?
5–10 cm H₂O — to overcome artificial-airway resistance and keep the spontaneous rate < 25/min with acceptable work of breathing.

cards.q: Initial FiO₂ when no SaO₂/PaO₂ data are available? Then titrate to what?
cards.a:
Initial FiO₂ when no SaO₂/PaO₂ data are available? Then titrate to what?
Start at 60–100%, then titrate to PaO₂ ≥ 60 torr or SaO₂ ≥ 92%. ARDS: FiO₂/PEEP combinations per protocol.

cards.q: Initial PEEP for adult full support? Then titrate to what?
cards.a:
Initial PEEP for adult full support? Then titrate to what?
5–10 cm H₂O, then as needed to keep SaO₂ ≥ 92% with FiO₂ ≤ 50% (and to balance auto-PEEP).

cards.q: Initial pressure limit in pressure control?
cards.a:
Initial pressure limit in pressure control?
20–30 cm H₂O, adjusted to reach the target expired VT (6–8 mL/kg PBW).

cards.q: What initial VT does the NBRC generally expect, and who is the exception?
cards.a:
What initial VT does the NBRC generally expect, and who is the exception?
6–8 mL/kg PBW for most patients — except acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (follow the NHLBI ARDS protocol).

cards.q: APRV initial settings: Plow, Phigh, Thigh, Tlow?
cards.a:
APRV initial settings: Plow, Phigh, Thigh, Tlow?
Plow 0–8 cm H₂O
Phigh for 4–8 mL/kg PBW, kept < 30–35 cm H₂O
Thigh 3–5 s
Tlow 0.2–0.8 s → about 10–20 cycles/min

cards.q: Which patients can be placed on APRV?
cards.a:
Which patients can be placed on APRV?
Only patients who can spontaneously trigger enough breaths to maintain adequate minute ventilation.

cards.q: What pH do you target on the ventilator, and how far can you let it drift?
cards.a:
What pH do you target on the ventilator, and how far can you let it drift?
Goal 7.35–7.45; depending on the problem, as low as 7.25 or as high as 7.50.

cards.q: To fix the pH, what do you change first — rate or VT? What are the limits?
cards.a:
To fix the pH, what do you change first — rate or VT? What are the limits?
Rate first (keep 8–24/min, up to 35/min in acute lung injury). Then VT, kept at 4–8 mL/kg PBW with Pplat ≤ 30–35 cm H₂O.

cards.q: When do you use permissive hypercapnia, and what is the pH floor?
cards.a:
When do you use permissive hypercapnia, and what is the pH floor?
When pH stays < 7.30 with rate, VT and Pplat at their upper limits — let PaCO₂ rise as long as pH stays above 7.20–7.25.

cards.q: Ventilating a COPD patient with chronic CO₂ retention — what PaCO₂ may give a normal pH?
cards.a:
Ventilating a COPD patient with chronic CO₂ retention — what PaCO₂ may give a normal pH?
55 torr or higher. Target the PaCO₂ that normalizes the pH, not 40 torr.

cards.q: Volume-control A/C: how do you LOWER PaCO₂? How do you RAISE it?
cards.a:
Volume-control A/C: how do you LOWER PaCO₂? How do you RAISE it?
Lower PaCO₂: ↑ rate (keep ≤ 24/min) or ↑ VT (keep Pplat < 30–35)
Raise PaCO₂: ↓ rate (keep ≥ 8/min), add mechanical deadspace, or ↓ VT if > 8 mL/kg

cards.q: Pressure control or APRV: which settings change the PaCO₂?
cards.a:
Pressure control or APRV: which settings change the PaCO₂?
PC: set rate and ΔP (PIP − PEEP)
APRV: release frequency (Thigh) and ΔP (Phigh − Plow)

cards.q: VT is already 6–8 mL/kg PBW with Pplat < 30. How should you change minute ventilation?
cards.a:
VT is already 6–8 mL/kg PBW with Pplat < 30. How should you change minute ventilation?
Change the rate — rate changes are the preferred method once VT is set properly.

cards.q: Acceptable PaO₂ / SaO₂ on the ventilator — most patients vs COPD or ARDS?
cards.a:
Acceptable PaO₂ / SaO₂ on the ventilator — most patients vs COPD or ARDS?
Most: PaO₂ ≥ 65 torr and SaO₂ ≥ 92%
COPD or ARDS: PaO₂ as low as 55 torr if SaO₂ ≥ 88%
(The initial-settings table uses PaO₂ ≥ 60 torr or SaO₂ ≥ 92% as the FiO₂ titration target.)

cards.q: Besides PaO₂/SaO₂, what hemoglobin level do you confirm for adequate oxygenation?
cards.a:
Besides PaO₂/SaO₂, what hemoglobin level do you confirm for adequate oxygenation?
Hb ≥ 10 g/dL — and confirm adequate circulation.

cards.q: Low PaO₂ on the ventilator: when do you raise FiO₂ and when do you raise PEEP?
cards.a:
Low PaO₂ on the ventilator: when do you raise FiO₂ and when do you raise PEEP?
Acceptable on < 50% O₂ → adjust FiO₂.
Can't stay acceptable on < 50% → adjust baseline pressure (PEEP / CPAP / Plow).

cards.q: What is the "60-60 rule" for hypoxemia?
cards.a:
What is the "60-60 rule" for hypoxemia?
PaO₂ > 60 on FiO₂ < 0.6 → V/Q mismatch → raise FiO₂
PaO₂ < 60 on FiO₂ > 0.6 → shunt → add/increase PEEP or CPAP

cards.q: Define refractory hypoxemia. How is it treated?
cards.a:
Define refractory hypoxemia. How is it treated?
PaO₂ ≤ 50 torr on FiO₂ ≥ 0.5 — treat with CPAP or PEEP. A P/F < 100 (e.g., PaO₂ < 60 on > 60% O₂) signals refractory hypoxemia and severe shunt/ARDS.

cards.q: When should you recommend the NHLBI ARDS protocol?
cards.a:
When should you recommend the NHLBI ARDS protocol?
P/F ≤ 200, or when ≥ 50% O₂ with PEEP ≥ 12 cm H₂O can't give acceptable PaO₂/SaO₂.

cards.q: Oxygenation is improving. Which do you lower first — FiO₂ or PEEP?
cards.a:
Oxygenation is improving. Which do you lower first — FiO₂ or PEEP?
FiO₂ first, down to ≤ 0.50 — then lower PEEP.

cards.q: What are the 5 ways to define "optimal PEEP"?
cards.a:
What are the 5 ways to define "optimal PEEP"?
The PEEP that:
1. Maximizes O₂ delivery
2. Gives the highest static compliance
3. Gives the biggest volume change for a given ΔP
4. Prevents alveolar collapse
5. Maximizes average expired tidal %CO₂

cards.q: On the NBRC exam, using SpO₂ and blood pressure — what is optimum PEEP?
cards.a:
On the NBRC exam, using SpO₂ and blood pressure — what is optimum PEEP?
The PEEP that keeps SpO₂ ≥ 88–90% without lowering blood pressure. Back off any PEEP increase that drops the BP significantly.

cards.q: In a volume-control PEEP study, which PEEP is optimal — and which number should you ignore?
cards.a:
In a volume-control PEEP study, which PEEP is optimal — and which number should you ignore?
The PEEP with the highest static compliance — the smallest Pplat − PEEP at constant VT. Ignore the PIP.

cards.q: Equal-pressure method (pressure control): how is optimal PEEP found?
cards.a:
Equal-pressure method (pressure control): how is optimal PEEP found?
Hold ΔP (PIP − PEEP) constant, typically 15–25 cm H₂O; the PEEP giving the largest exhaled VT is optimal.

cards.q: Static pressure–volume curve: where do you set PEEP?
cards.a:
Static pressure–volume curve: where do you set PEEP?
2–3 cm H₂O above the lower inflection point (LIP).

cards.q: Decremental PEEP after a recruitment maneuver: step size, wait time, and final setting?
cards.a:
Decremental PEEP after a recruitment maneuver: step size, wait time, and final setting?
Lower PEEP in 2 cm H₂O steps, waiting 3–5 minutes per step to measure CRS. Set PEEP 2 cm H₂O above the level that gave the highest CRS (after re-recruiting). Check ABGs after 20–30 minutes.

cards.q: Measuring static mechanics: what 2 conditions do you need?
cards.a:
Measuring static mechanics: what 2 conditions do you need?
Complete relaxation of the respiratory muscles and zero flow for at least 2–3 seconds so pressures equilibrate.

cards.q: Acute respiratory distress not due to heart failure: which 3 criteria mean you should consider the ARDSNet protocol?
cards.a:
Acute respiratory distress not due to heart failure: which 3 criteria mean you should consider the ARDSNet protocol?
P/F < 300
Bilateral diffuse infiltrates consistent with pulmonary edema
No clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension / LV failure

cards.q: ARDSNet: initial VT and how you get to the target VT?
cards.a:
ARDSNet: initial VT and how you get to the target VT?
Start at 8 mL/kg PBW, then reduce by 1 mL/kg at intervals ≤ 2 hours until 6 mL/kg PBW. Any mode, but keep I:E ≤ 1:1.

cards.q: ARDSNet: initial rate and maximum rate?
cards.a:
ARDSNet: initial rate and maximum rate?
Approximate the patient's baseline — generally 12–20/min, no greater than 35/min.

cards.q: ARDSNet oxygenation goal? Minimum PEEP?
cards.a:
ARDSNet oxygenation goal? Minimum PEEP?
PaO₂ 55–80 torr or SpO₂ 88–95%, using PEEP of at least 5–8 cm H₂O plus FiO₂/PEEP combinations.

cards.q: ARDSNet plateau pressure limit — and how often do you measure it?
cards.a:
ARDSNet plateau pressure limit — and how often do you measure it?
Pplat ≤ 30 cm H₂O, measured every 4 hours and after each PEEP or VT change.
Your course: Chang's printed slides use < 35 cm H₂O; the ARDSNet/modern target is < 30. Ask which your instructor keys.

cards.q: ARDSNet: Pplat > 30 — what now? Pplat < 25 with VT < 6 mL/kg — what now?
cards.a:
ARDSNet: Pplat > 30 — what now? Pplat < 25 with VT < 6 mL/kg — what now?
Pplat > 30: ↓ VT in 1 mL/kg steps, minimum 4 mL/kg
Pplat < 25 and VT < 6: ↑ VT by 1 mL/kg until Pplat > 25 or VT = 6 mL/kg

cards.q: ARDSNet: breath stacking/dyssynchrony with Pplat < 30. What can you do with VT?
cards.a:
ARDSNet: breath stacking/dyssynchrony with Pplat < 30. What can you do with VT?
Increase VT in 1 mL/kg steps up to 7–8 mL/kg, as long as Pplat stays < 30 cm H₂O.

cards.q: ARDSNet pH goal, and what you do at pH 7.15–7.30 vs < 7.15?
cards.a:
ARDSNet pH goal, and what you do at pH 7.15–7.30 vs < 7.15?
Goal 7.30–7.45
7.15–7.30: ↑ rate until pH > 7.30 or PaCO₂ < 25 (max rate 35)
< 7.15: rate to 35; still < 7.15 → ↑ VT by 1 mL/kg (Pplat may be exceeded), consider NaHCO₃

cards.q: When do you recommend prone positioning in ARDS, and for how long?
cards.a:
When do you recommend prone positioning in ARDS, and for how long?
Severe ARDS: P/F < 150 with FiO₂ > 60% and PEEP ≥ 5 cm H₂O. Most effective for at least 16 hours per day.

cards.q: Weaning an adult off HFOV: FiO₂ target, Pmean steps, and when to switch to PC?
cards.a:
Weaning an adult off HFOV: FiO₂ target, Pmean steps, and when to switch to PC?
Lower FiO₂ to 0.40, then drop Pmean 2–3 cm H₂O every 4–6 hours until ≤ 20 cm H₂O. Then switch to PC with a limit ≤ 30 and PEEP 10–12 cm H₂O.

cards.q: BiPAP initial settings: IPAP, EPAP, backup rate, target VT?
cards.a:
BiPAP initial settings: IPAP, EPAP, backup rate, target VT?
IPAP 10–15 cm H₂O
EPAP 5 cm H₂O
Backup rate at least 8/min
Aim for VT 6–8 mL/kg

cards.q: Why keep IPAP below 20–25 cm H₂O?
cards.a:
Why keep IPAP below 20–25 cm H₂O?
That is the esophageal opening pressure — higher IPAP causes gastric insufflation.

cards.q: On BiPAP, what do you change to fix PaCO₂? To fix oxygenation?
cards.a:
On BiPAP, what do you change to fix PaCO₂? To fix oxygenation?
PaCO₂/pH: IPAP or ΔP (IPAP − EPAP) — ↑ to lower PaCO₂
PaO₂/SaO₂: FiO₂ and EPAP (keep ΔP constant so PaCO₂ doesn't change)

cards.q: On BiPAP: PaO₂ ≤ 50 torr on FiO₂ ≥ 0.50. What do you do?
cards.a:
On BiPAP: PaO₂ ≤ 50 torr on FiO₂ ≥ 0.50. What do you do?
That's shunting → raise EPAP (keep ΔP constant). If FiO₂ < 0.50 with simple V/Q mismatch, raise FiO₂ instead.

cards.q: BiPAP FiO₂/EPAP target?
cards.a:
BiPAP FiO₂/EPAP target?
PaO₂ ≥ 65 torr or SaO₂ ≥ 92%

cards.q: Below what pH should BiPAP generally NOT be used?
cards.a:
Below what pH should BiPAP generally NOT be used?
pH < 7.20 (along with arrest, uncooperative patient, excess secretions, aspiration risk, upper-airway obstruction, hemodynamic instability…)

cards.q: "BiPAP 5/10" vs "CPAP + PS 5 + 10" — what are the PIP and ΔP for each?
cards.a:
"BiPAP 5/10" vs "CPAP + PS 5 + 10" — what are the PIP and ΔP for each?
CPAP + PS 5 + 10: PIP 15, ΔP 10 cm H₂O (PS rides on top of CPAP)
BiPAP 5/10: PIP (= IPAP) 10, ΔP only 5 cm H₂O

cards.q: BiPAP timed mode: starting %I-time?
cards.a:
BiPAP timed mode: starting %I-time?
20–30%

cards.q: NPPV weaning readiness: which rate, heart rate, pressures, pH and SpO₂?
cards.a:
NPPV weaning readiness: which rate, heart rate, pressures, pH and SpO₂?
RR < 25/min, HR < 110/min
IPAP < 15, EPAP < 10 cm H₂O
Compensated pH > 7.35
SpO₂ > 90% on < 50%

cards.q: How do you wean from NPPV?
cards.a:
How do you wean from NPPV?
Start in daytime, progressively extend time off (meals, fluids, airway clearance, skin care). After daytime success, give at least one more night of support.

cards.q: Adult ventilator apnea delay alarm setting?
cards.a:
Adult ventilator apnea delay alarm setting?
20 seconds

cards.q: Low-pressure alarm setting?
cards.a:
Low-pressure alarm setting?
8 cm H₂O, or 5–10 cm H₂O below PIP (in SIMV use the PIP of the pressure-supported breaths).

cards.q: High-pressure limit setting?
cards.a:
High-pressure limit setting?
50 cm H₂O, or 10–15 cm H₂O above PIP (in SIMV use the mandatory breaths' PIP).

cards.q: Low PEEP/CPAP alarm setting?
cards.a:
Low PEEP/CPAP alarm setting?
3–5 cm H₂O below set PEEP

cards.q: Low exhaled VT alarm setting?
cards.a:
Low exhaled VT alarm setting?
100 mL, or 10–15% below set VT (or spontaneous VT in SIMV/CPAP)

cards.q: Low and high minute ventilation alarm settings?
cards.a:
Low and high minute ventilation alarm settings?
Low V̇E: 4–5 L/min, or 10–15% below the minimum SIMV/A/C
High V̇E: 10–15% above baseline

cards.q: O₂ analyzer and humidifier temperature alarm limits?
cards.a:
O₂ analyzer and humidifier temperature alarm limits?
O₂ analyzer: ±5–6% of set FiO₂
Temperature: ±2°C of set, never above 41°C

cards.q: High-pressure alarm — common causes?
cards.a:
High-pressure alarm — common causes?
↑ Resistance / ↓ compliance · airway obstruction · cough, secretions, mucus plugs · patient–ventilator asynchrony · anxiety, restlessness, pain

cards.q: Low-pressure alarm — common causes?
cards.a:
Low-pressure alarm — common causes?
Disconnection · airway/circuit leaks · alarm set above the PS breath's PIP · improved compliance and resistance

cards.q: Which alarms must every acute-care NPPV ventilator have?
cards.a:
Which alarms must every acute-care NPPV ventilator have?
Low-pressure/disconnect and power failure.

cards.q: Normal respiratory-system compliance — by plethysmography vs during mechanical ventilation?
cards.a:
Normal respiratory-system compliance — by plethysmography vs during mechanical ventilation?
Plethysmography: about 100 mL/cm H₂O
On the ventilator: lower, 40–80 mL/cm H₂O
Your course: Your Chang decks print static compliance 60–100 mL/cm H₂O — a different (non-intubated) population, not a contradiction.

cards.q: Normal airway resistance — healthy subject vs intubated patient?
cards.a:
Normal airway resistance — healthy subject vs intubated patient?
Healthy (plethysmography): 1–3 cm H₂O/L/sec
The artificial airway adds at least 4–6; significantly above 5–9 suggests obstruction.
(The formula appendix gives 5–15 as the orally intubated normal.)
Your course: Your weaning deck prints 0.6–2.4 cm H₂O/L/sec (non-intubated).

cards.q: Formulas: static compliance, dynamic compliance, airway resistance?
cards.a:
Formulas: static compliance, dynamic compliance, airway resistance?
Crs (static) = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP)
Cdyn = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP)
Raw = (PIP − Pplat) ÷ flow (L/sec)

cards.q: How does Cdyn compare with Crs, and what does the gap between them mean?
cards.a:
How does Cdyn compare with Crs, and what does the gap between them mean?
Cdyn is always less than Crs. The difference (Crs − Cdyn) is due to airway resistance — the bigger the gap, the more resistance.

cards.q: VT 700 mL, PEEP 8, PIP 42, Pplat 35 cm H₂O. Static compliance?
cards.a:
VT 700 mL, PEEP 8, PIP 42, Pplat 35 cm H₂O. Static compliance?
700 ÷ (35 − 8) = 26 mL/cm H₂O (low — normal on the vent is 40–80)

cards.q: VT 400 mL, flow 75 L/min, PEEP 6, PIP 45, Pplat 30. Airway resistance?
cards.a:
VT 400 mL, flow 75 L/min, PEEP 6, PIP 45, Pplat 30. Airway resistance?
75 L/min ÷ 60 = 1.25 L/sec → (45 − 30) ÷ 1.25 = 12 cm H₂O/L/sec

cards.q: Volume control: compliance DROPS (Raw unchanged). What happens to PIP, Pplat and PIP − Pplat?
cards.a:
Volume control: compliance DROPS (Raw unchanged). What happens to PIP, Pplat and PIP − Pplat?
↑ PIP, ↑ Pplat, PIP − Pplat unchanged, ↓ Cdyn, flatter pressure–volume loop.

cards.q: Volume control: resistance RISES (compliance unchanged). What happens to PIP, Pplat and PIP − Pplat?
cards.a:
Volume control: resistance RISES (compliance unchanged). What happens to PIP, Pplat and PIP − Pplat?
↑ PIP, ↑ PIP − Pplat, Pplat unchanged, ↓ Cdyn, wider pressure–volume loop.

cards.q: Pressure control: compliance drops. What do you see?
cards.a:
Pressure control: compliance drops. What do you see?
Decreased tidal volume (and a flatter pressure–volume loop).

cards.q: Normal work of breathing for a healthy adult?
cards.a:
Normal work of breathing for a healthy adult?
0.5–0.7 joules/L

cards.q: How do you detect and measure auto-PEEP?
cards.a:
How do you detect and measure auto-PEEP?
Not visible on the pressure–time graph — look at the flow–time waveform (or flow–volume loop). Measure it with an end-expiratory pause: the baseline pressure rises to the trapped alveolar pressure.

cards.q: Auto-PEEP from high rate / short E-time: 4 fixes? From small-airway collapse: what then?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP from high rate / short E-time: 4 fixes? From small-airway collapse: what then?
↓ rate · ↑ inspiratory flow (VC) · ↓ VT (VC) · ↓ inspiratory time (PC)
Airway collapse / high compliance → add external PEEP up to 50–80% of measured auto-PEEP.

cards.q: Rate 20/min with I:E 1:4. Total cycle time, inspiratory time, expiratory time?
cards.a:
Rate 20/min with I:E 1:4. Total cycle time, inspiratory time, expiratory time?
Cycle time = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 s
TI = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 s
TE = 3 − 0.6 = 2.4 s

cards.q: TI 2 s, TE 3 s. What is the I:E ratio?
cards.a:
TI 2 s, TE 3 s. What is the I:E ratio?
I:E = 1 : (3 ÷ 2) = 1:1.5
